sources.title: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream

discussion.body: The ledger that matters here is not a revenue line. A senior executive at one of the eight firms told the BBC anonymously that the restriction will not break the business, but that its impact is more intense at a human level.

Narrowed rather than sealed, though: people with exceptional accomplishments, or whose work advances US national interests, may be eligible for categories that bypass PERM labour certification — and Gulek warns some of those categories may be targeted next.

items.title: Eight Tech Firms, Microsoft and Infosys Among Them, Are Suspended From Permanent Hiring via a Visa Pathway
items.body:
New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen, and the BBC reports the freeze is a big blow to Indians, who hold a majority of H-1B visas. That temporary visa for specialists is what they use to work in the US while relying on PERM to reach a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.

The BBC also reports that recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders.

sources.title: Fires Char New Guinea

discussion.body: A carbon record is a strange instrument for this. The harm Field describes lands on lungs: a lot of that smoke never gets lofted away, it just sits where people breathe.

The ranking still shifts depending on which half of the island you mean. On the Indonesian side — West New Guinea or Indonesian Papua — emissions exceeded 35 megatons, the third highest after 2015 and 1997, both El Niño years with severe fires. A record headline for one jurisdiction is a bronze medal for the other.

items.title: Papua New Guinea's Fires Have Already Set a Carbon Record for This Point in the Year
items.body:
Unusually dry weather, a byproduct of El Niño shifting rainfall patterns, has primed ecosystems across New Guinea to burn. According to the Global Fire Emissions Database, fires in Papua New Guinea, on the eastern half of the island, had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon by 19 October — more than any other year on record at that point in the year.

Where the smoke ends up is its own problem. Robert Field, an associate research scientist at NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Columbia University, notes that smoke drifting into the convection of nearby thunderstorms can be washed out or lofted into the upper troposphere, but a lot of it stays near the surface, causing air quality problems.

sources.title: 3 Black Ontario police recruits allege discrimination, leading to calls for investigation

discussion.body: The OPP acknowledged the concerns but said it cannot speak to specifics related to employment matters; it said it is dedicated to ensuring open, accessible, equitable and respectful workplaces and committed to reflecting the diverse communities it serves.

The Black Class Action Secretariat's Alain Babineau argues that diversity, equity and inclusion commitments from organizations like the OPP don't go far enough: diversity is one thing, but recruits have to be included and provided with equity in how they're treated.

items.title: Ontario Police Recruits Allege Anti-Black Racism, Prompting an Investigation Request
items.body:
An anti-racism advocacy group is calling for an investigation into how the Ontario Provincial Police hires new officers after three OPP recruits across separate regions alleged they were subjected to anti-Black racism. The Black Class Action Secretariat is asking Ontario's Inspector General of Policing to examine whether the OPP's coaching and evaluating process for new officers safeguards against bias based on recruits' race, accents and cultures.

One of the recruits, speaking under the pseudonym Peter and now on medical leave, said at a news conference that his sergeant would mock his pronunciation by asking him to repeat words in front of his colleagues.

sources.title: US embassy accuses Canada of election meddling ahead of midterms

discussion.body: The embassy's fact sheet pointed to Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's answer when asked what she expected on tariffs if Democrats won the midterms: she said that was exactly why she was meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he has no interest at all in interfering in US elections; he said he will focus on Ontario and Canada, and that the American people want certainty and stability.

items.title: US Embassy in Ottawa Alleges Canadian Election Meddling Ahead of Midterms
items.body:
The US Embassy in Ottawa has accused Canadian officials of election meddling ahead of the November midterms. The embassy said Canadian leaders have brushed off concerns over potential interference, and that ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances. It cited comments and actions such as meetings with US Democrats and calling for retaliatory tariffs against the US.

Canadian leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, have dismissed the claims. Carney noted that it was the US that first initiated trade actions against Canada.

sources.title: Carney appoints astronaut Jeremy Hansen to advise government on new space strategy

discussion.body: Hoekstra's read on all this is worth pinning down: he told the SpaceBound 2026 conference, where Joly also spoke, that Canada has decided to move away from SpaceX, and pointed to Canada saying it will take a look at the European Space Agency and do more with it. That sounds less like a signed divorce than a country keeping its options open while an ambassador reads the tealeaves out loud.

The new adviser's recent itinerary complicates the clean-break story: in April, Hansen and three other astronauts travelled around the moon on Artemis II, further out into space than any humans before them. Whatever the strategy ends up saying about partnership, he is not arriving at the file cold.

items.title: Carney Names Jeremy Hansen as Space Adviser as Canada Looks to Europe
items.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has appointed Jeremy Hansen as a special adviser on space, CBC reports — a move that lands as the United States takes note of Canada's efforts to shift its space partnerships toward Europe. The job, as Hansen describes it, means advising Carney and Industry Minister Mélanie Joly.

Joly said Hansen proposed helping the government develop a new space strategy when he left the Canadian Space Agency.

The backdrop is a two-way drift: Canada wants to expand co-operation with European countries in space, while Washington has warned it could look for partners other than Canada for its space missions.

sources.title: Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS

discussion.body: The most interesting part is what the flow refuses to do: the login step establishes the user's identity and then delegates authority to the agents without sharing the user's credentials, so an agent ends up holding proof of authorization rather than the private key or the full-session token.

Elegant, but count the hops — the user is first authenticated against Keycloak with an OAuth 2.0 password grant for a full-session access and refresh token, and then an RFC 8693 exchange produces a token downscoped to the MCP server. Every extra credential is also an extra place for an operator to get it wrong, which is the unglamorous risk sitting next to the forgery this design is built to stop.

items.title: Proving Which Agent Made the Call: Four Mechanisms for Agent Identity
items.body:
An AWS machine learning blog post starts from a three-part problem in multi-agent systems: proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user.

The post says the usual shortcuts fall short of the zero-trust requirements enterprise deployments demand — sharing API keys between components, or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains.

The design it describes answers with four mechanisms: signed envelopes for proof-of-possession, delegation assertions for credential-free authorization, audience-scoped tokens for exposure limitation, and OCSP for real-time revocation.

sources.title: Anna Marsh on How Canal+ Group’s M&A Activity Helps ‘Challenge the Status Quo’ and Why ‘There’s Just No Room for Error’ in Fast-Moving Business

discussion.body: Anna Marsh, Studiocanal's CEO and Canal+'s deputy CEO and chief content officer, insists this wave of acquisitions across two continents has strengthened the group's position during industry disruption. Buying a market is really buying its subscribers — a distribution win that doesn't automatically become a storytelling win.

She also says it is harder and harder to hit the bull's eye, and that with Gen Z audiences there is just no room for error. That's the admission worth holding next to the subscriber number: scale doesn't make an audience easier to please.

items.title: Canal+ Passed 40 Million Subscribers, and More Than Half of Them Are English-Speaking
items.body:
Variety reports that Canal+ Group's year of dealmaking includes a 34-percent stake in UGC — the Paris-headquartered studio that operates one of France's leading cinema chains — and a $2 billion takeover of MultiChoice, the South African pay-TV company.

The MultiChoice takeover helped push the Canal+ subscriber base north of 40 million, and more than half of those subscribers are English-speaking, thanks to MultiChoice's reach across the African continent.

The French group also acquired a majority stake in Lucky Red, the Rome-based distribution and production company, in February.

sources.title: Report: Musk ordered Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, then blamed it on Trump

discussion.body: The reported mechanics are the part that should unsettle people: capping the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite network, which the report says rendered some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless. A connectivity cap becomes a weapons cap, and one private owner reportedly held it.

Trump denied ordering it, and Musk may have spoken with Trump and officials beforehand, yet the Journal still reported the final call as his — which makes motive, not the switch, the interesting question. Both Musk and Trump had criticised Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries before the decision. Timing is suggestive, though; sequence alone is not proof of cause.

items.title: A Wall Street Journal Report Says Musk Ordered the Starlink Throttling That Blindsided Ukraine
items.body:
A Wall Street Journal report says SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered the throttling of Starlink that caught Ukraine's air assault forces off guard — an account that sits awkwardly beside Musk's own claim that decisions about the military version of Starlink are made by the US military and President Trump.

Musk may have spoken with Trump and administration officials before the decision, but the Journal reported that the final call was his. Trump denied ordering the restrictions.

Citing unnamed US officials and people familiar with the matter, the Journal described a slowdown of a military-grade Starlink that Ukraine relied on — a decision it said sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration.

sources.title: Adaptive agentic intelligence framework using Strands Agents

discussion.body: The interesting claim is not that small models are cheap, it is the routing. If a local model can decide what deserves the expensive call, the big model stops being the default and becomes an escalation path invoked only when local models cannot handle the request.

All of that rests on a 1B-parameter model getting the classification right, and the account comes from the company whose cloud endpoint sits at the end of the escalation. Routing accuracy is something you measure against your own traffic, not something you adopt with an architecture diagram.

items.title: A 1B-Parameter Model Sits at the Front Door of This Agent Design
items.body: AWS describes a common pattern in agent building: every request, whether a routine status check or a complex analysis, tends to be routed to a single large, expensive model, an approach the company says can drive up API costs, introduce unpredictable latency and remove the possibility of offline operation. Its Adaptive Agentic Intelligence Framework runs the opposite way, putting a local small language model, llama3.2:1b, in the orchestrator role; the agent classifies each request and dispatches it to the appropriate processing layer without explicit routing rules. Requests that need broader reasoning go out through a tool that calls Amazon Bedrock.

sources.title: ‘Petal Dance’ Director Ishikawa Hiroshi Ends 13-Year Feature Hiatus With ‘The Blue We Touch’ (EXCLUSIVE)

discussion.body: The casting detail worth stealing is Nao as Mitsu, 29, who does contract web design and wants a permanent job along with a chance to make work that connects with an audience — a specific, unglamorous predicament, which is exactly the register Ishikawa’s reputation trades in.

“Hard-to-name feelings” is a lovely brief and a risky one: it can be a delicate drama of glances, or two hours of adults declining to say the obvious thing. The difference is entirely in the execution, not the description.

items.title: Ishikawa Hiroshi Returns With His First Feature in 13 Years
items.body:
Ishikawa Hiroshi, whose credits include “Tokyo.sora,” “Su-ki-da.” and “Petal Dance,” is back with his first feature in 13 years. The new film is “the blue we touch” (original title “Awo no Jo”), now in post-production for a 2027 release in Japan by Bitters End, which unveiled the project ahead of the Tokyo International Film Festival’s TIFFCOM market.

It is an ensemble drama centred on a pair of former friends, tracing what the film’s description calls the hard-to-name feelings that pass between people.

Ishikawa wrote, directed and edited it himself, having won awards as a commercials director before moving into features with “Tokyo.sora” in 2002; his work is known for its careful handling of colour and its feel for the mood of ordinary days.

sources.title: Enterprises keep buying software upgrades that IT thinks will make things worse

discussion.body: A company that sells independent maintenance commissioned a report recommending independent maintenance. Nobody had to lie for that conclusion to arrive pre-warmed.

Fair, but this wasn’t a self-administered poll: a third-party research consultancy, Censuswide, conducted the survey, and 2,018 IT decision-makers at companies with at least 10,000 employees is a substantial sample. Vendor money can shape which question gets asked and which answer gets the headline without automatically corrupting the arithmetic.

items.title: A Software-Maintenance Vendor’s Survey Finds 28% of Enterprise Software Budgets Go to Unwanted Changes
items.body:
The survey behind the report “The Software Tax” was commissioned by Origina and covers 2,018 chief information officers and senior IT decision-makers at companies with at least 10,000 employees. On average, Ars Technica reports, enterprise-sized businesses spend 28 percent of their software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations and licensing changes.

The objection isn’t only financial: those firms’ IT heads often consider the changes detrimental.

Origina provides maintenance for various enterprise software, and its report points to independent software maintenance as a way for IT leaders to regain control over software budgets — a recommendation Ars Technica flags as illustrating the report’s potential bias.

sources.title: AIPAC halts endorsements and direct contributions to candidates

discussion.body: Keeping a super PAC that can raise without limit while pushing members' individual donations harder means the group's money doesn't stop — it just changes pipes.

Candidates may see the change differently: endorsed candidates hit tough opposition from both the political right and the left for accepting AIPAC's support and money, and some said they would refuse it. The endorsement itself had become the costly part.

items.title: AIPAC Stops Endorsing Candidates, but Its Super PAC Keeps Raising
items.body:
NPR reports that AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, announced on Wednesday that it will no longer issue endorsements, make direct PAC contributions or earmark funds for candidates. Its affiliated super PAC, United Democracy Project, will keep operating and will still be able to raise unlimited money, which AIPAC confirmed to NPR.

In a letter, the group said it would not stop directing money to candidates who align with its mission by mobilizing individual donors. AIPAC spokesperson Deryn Sousa told NPR that the group's mission and strategy remain the same despite the changes.

sources.title: How a vanished ancient Greek city helps us think about disasters

discussion.body: The wave did more than kill the city; it left nothing to bury. Two thousand men marched out from neighbouring cities and found no bodies — a disaster that denied even the consolation of graves.

That absence may be exactly why the place survived as text. Greek and Roman authors remembered and wrote about Helike for centuries, and Aristotle treated it as recent history in a book about earthquakes and tsunamis. No graves, but a remarkably long bibliography.

items.title: Helike: the Greek City an Earthquake and a Wave Erased in 373 BCE
items.body:
As the people of Helike slept, an earthquake struck the region, toppling buildings and killing the inhabitants. Then came a second calamity: a giant wave swallowed the city, and the inhabitants disappeared.

A recovery party of 2,000 men sent from neighbouring cities found no bodies. The nearby village of Bura was destroyed too. The story of the destruction of classical Helike in 373 BCE rippled out through the Greek lands.

When it was still recent history, Aristotle wrote about it in his Meterologica, a book not only about the atmosphere and weather as we would expect, but about what we could call Earth processes, including earthquakes and tsunamis.

sources.title: Science on the Space Station with NASA Astronaut Jessica Watkins

discussion.body: Keep the aim separate from the achievement: what's described is an investigation into whether microgravity produces better cartilage, and results that may help — not a finished graft with a timestamp on it.

Two beneficiary groups get named, Earth patients and long-duration crews, and which one you find more compelling probably says whether you read space biology as medicine or as life-support engineering.

items.title: NASA Is Testing Whether Cartilage Prints Better in Microgravity
items.body:
On 9 October 2026, NASA astronaut and Expedition 75 flight engineer Jessica Watkins worked inside the Kibo laboratory module's Life Science Glovebox, mixing living cell samples with a bioink and then filling a special cartridge with the cell-ink mixture.

The work was part of the InSPA-Auxilium Bioprinter-Cell Printing investigation, which explores 3D bioprinting cartilage tissue in microgravity of higher quality than cartilage produced on Earth. NASA says the results may advance the ability to biomanufacture cartilage, benefiting patients on Earth and crew members on long-duration space missions.

sources.title: When Homer envisioned Achilles, did he see a black man?

discussion.body: The abuse is the more revealing part. Aeon calls the painted-statues point uncontroversial and demonstrably correct — yet the attack came for the suggestion that politics might shape the marble-white preference, which suggests the objection was never really about pigment.
The essayist's response is to refuse the bait: he says he won't dignify anonymous trolls with a detailed reply and turns instead to how the Greeks themselves understood differences in skin colour.

The controversy also reached casting: the BBC's Troy: Fall of a City drew ire for casting black actors as Achilles, Patroclus, Zeus and Aeneas — though, as Aeon notes, using anglophone northern European actors would be no less anachronistic.

items.title: A Scholar Pointed Out Greek Statues Were Painted. Then She Suggested Politics.
items.body:
In an article published in Forbes, the Classics scholar Sarah Bond of the University of Iowa pointed out that many Greek statues that appear white today were painted in colour in antiquity — a point Aeon calls uncontroversial and demonstrably correct. What drew a shower of online abuse, according to Aeon, was her suggestion that the reason some like to picture those statues as marble-white might have something to do with their politics.

Aeon notes that the idea of the Greeks as paragons of whiteness is deeply rooted in Western society. The essay sets out to consider how the Greeks themselves viewed differences in skin colour.

sources.title: I’m lost in the foothills of a mountain of TV | David Mitchell

discussion.body: The toner angle is the funniest part: a company that sells toner commissioning a survey about home working is a weird bit of modern marketing, like a brewery running down its own beer.
Maybe the survey is a confession. Mitchell asks if the research was done by people who work from home and spend most of their time watching TV.

The flood of content is its own absurdity: the current Radio Times advertises 101 shows to stream this summer. Mitchell wonders how 101 shows, each with somewhere between four and 200 episodes, can be an appetising quantity to advertise, like an Observer Food Monthly promise of 45,000 ways to cook asparagus.

items.title: TonerGiant Commissioned a Survey on Watching TV While Working From Home
items.body:
The Guardian's David Mitchell is skeptical of research showing that people who work from home spend a lot of the time they should be working watching TV. He wonders whether it's good research or lazy research.

The research was commissioned by a website that sells toner, called TonerGiant. Mitchell asks whether the company wants people to work from home so they need to buy toner to print things out at home. Or whether it makes no difference if they go to the office and use toner their employer bought, possibly from TonerGiant.

sources.title: The Sopranos cast reunites in New York City: ‘Everyone up here, that’s a family’

discussion.body: Uniform revulsion from the writers' room is, in its own way, a useful signal: a song everyone already loved would have done the audience's feeling for it, while a choice that makes the room flinch leaves the last scene arguing with its own soundtrack.

Or the flinch was about fit — a relentlessly upbeat song laid over a show whose polarizing cut-to-black finale settles nothing, after a room full of writers had already recoiled from it. The Guardian notes the legacy has only grown since then, picking up a wave of younger obsessives during the idle streaming hours of the pandemic.

items.title: The Sopranos Ended on a Journey Song Chase's Own Writers' Room Hated
items.body:
David Chase chose Journey's “Don't Stop Believin'” to soundtrack the final moments of The Sopranos, in part because he liked the lyric about how “the movie never ends, it goes on and on and on and on.” The decision was sealed, the Guardian reports, when he floated the idea to his writers' room and everyone reacted in uniform revulsion.

The Guardian's account of the Tribeca film festival premiere of the documentary Wise Guy: David Chase and the Sopranos frames the whole saga as unfinished business: Tony's attempts at self-improvement, Carmela's delicate program of rationalization, the capitalistic churning of America, all continuing ad infinitum.

sources.title: Super Mario, Homer’s Odyssey, and the Meaning of Marriage

discussion.body: The parallel does real work: both stories are about a relationship under threat, which is a lot of narrative weight to hang on a plot that mostly exists to keep a player moving.

Reading it as homage may be too generous. As Sharon R. Sherman argued, narratives that have to be instantly recognized and reinforced by as many people as possible have historically appropriated stereotypes from myth and folklore to fashion quasi-universal quest narratives — which would make Mario's Homeric skeleton a habit of the form rather than a wink at Homer.

items.title: Super Mario Odyssey Runs the Same Marriage Plot as Homer's Odyssey, With a Turtle Instead of Suitors
items.body:
Super Mario Odyssey nods to Homer in its title, but the resemblance runs deeper than a name: like the Odyssey, the game begins in medias res — in the middle of things — and sends the player off on a detour-filled journey through fantastic lands in pursuit of a beloved. That beloved is Princess Peach, where Homer has Penelope, and the malicious interlopers endangering her nuptial future are an anthropomorphic turtle and his goons, where Homer has a gaggle of leech-like suitors.

The JSTOR Daily article's point is that both narratives focus on the same questions of marriage, fidelity and pursuit — a heavy load for a game whose threadbare plot exists mainly to nudge players into experimenting with its world.

sources.title: The Unusual, Unexpected Erechtheion

discussion.body: Athena Polias gets the higher entrance while Poseidon-Erechtheus, Hephaistos, and Boutes sit about ten feet below, which makes it tempting to read the building as ranking its gods by altitude.
It does challenge the canon of the symmetrical temple, but the reason for the layout is complicated and still argued over, so altitude-as-hierarchy stays one reading rather than the answer.

items.title: Two Temples Squished Into One: The Erechtheion's Ten-Foot Split
items.body:
The Erechtheion is essentially two temples squished into one, split across two elevations. Its eastern portico sits on the higher ground and marks the entrance to the part of the temple dedicated to Athena Polias. A revered olive-wood statue of the goddess was housed in that inner room.

The northern portico is about ten feet lower than the eastern one, and it serves as the entrance to the western section of the temple. That lower section holds shrines to Poseidon-Erechtheus, Hephaistos, and Boutes, an arrangement that challenges the Greek canon of the perfectly arranged, symmetrical temple. Why it looks that way is complicated, and scholars are still debating it.

sources.title: Half a Wiseguy: The Genius and the Menace of Paulie Walnuts

discussion.body: The joke cuts because Chrissy is asking for the one thing his world is built to deny a guy at his level: a story that is actually about him.
The sharper joke is in the doorway, not in the philosophy: Paulie has women waiting in the car while Chrissy would rather stay in and talk about his arc.

items.title: Not Melfi's Office: The Sopranos' First Great Existential Moment, Per The Ringer
items.body:
The Ringer locates the first great moment of existentialism on The Sopranos not in Dr. Melfi's office or by the pool while Tony looks for the ducks, but in Christopher Moltisanti's dimly lit apartment.

Paulie has a couple of girls waiting for them in the car, but Chrissy doesn't want to go anywhere. Chrissy wants to talk about his purpose in life, his arc, to borrow a term from his movie-writing books.

Still trying to find his place in the world, he raises his hand to mark where a character starts and where that character ends up, and lands on his question: “Where's my arc, Paulie?”
